one_liner: Header-only C++ JSON library that parses straight into your typed structs, beating RapidJSON, simdjson DOM, Boost.JSON and nlohmann.
what_it_does: Solves typed JSON (de)serialization by parsing each member directly into the target C++ type's constructor arguments in one pass, instead of building an intermediate DOM. You map a type once via a `json_data_contract` specialization (or, on newer toolchains, C++26 static reflection / Boost.PFR / Boost.Describe adapters for automatic mapping), then call `daw::json::from_json<T>`/`to_json`. It also ships a lazy pull (`json_value`) DOM-like view, a SAX push parser, an array iterator for large documents, and NDJSON/JSON-Lines iteration with thread partitioning.
how_it_is_fast: No allocation inside the parser itself (memory shown in kostya's table is +0.00 MiB over baseline, versus +175 MiB for simdjson DOM and +96 MiB for gason); allocation, if any, happens only in the resulting user types. It skips DOM/tree construction entirely, parsing directly to constructor args in declaration order, and backtracks only if struct member order doesn't match JSON key order. Numeric parsing uses the Eisel-Lemire fast path for doubles and the Dragonbox algorithm for float-to-string; optional SSE4.2/AVX2/NEON paths exist for member-skip scanning, though the README says the constexpr non-SIMD path is often faster.
when_to_use: JSON schema is fixed and known at compile time, and you want to build typed C++ objects without an intermediate DOM
You need to construct immutable or non-default-constructible types straight from JSON via their constructors
You want strictly bounded/zero parser-side allocation (embedded, latency-sensitive, or `-fno-exceptions` builds via `DAW_JSON_DONT_USE_EXCEPTIONS`)
You're streaming large arrays or NDJSON/JSON-Lines files and want a thread-partitioning iterator built in
You also need SAX-style minification, JSON Path lookups, or JSON Schema generation from the same mapping
when_not_to_use: You want a drop-in mutable DOM you can edit and reserialize with zero setup (nlohmann::json-style) rather than declaring a mapping per type
Compile-time budget is tight: heavy template metaprogramming for the mapping machinery adds to build times
Raw parse throughput is the only goal and DOM/typed structure doesn't matter: simdjson On-Demand beats it in the same kostya table (0.060s vs 0.089s g++)

You need certified-accurate float parsing on adversarial inputs: kostya's README flags DAW JSON Link (checked variant) among libraries with known number-parsing inaccuracies (issue #226, still open as a research note citing Clinger's accurate-parsing paper, not confirmed fixed)
Your team wants minimal per-type boilerplate and doesn't already use C++26 reflection or Boost.PFR/Describe for automatic mapping

integration.dependencies: daw::header_libraries and daw::utf_range (both header-only, same author, pulled automatically via CMake FetchContent from extern/CMakeLists.txt)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 minimum (tested GCC 9-12, Clang 8-14, MSVC 19.29); C++20 enables inline NTTP member names; C++26 static reflection (or Boost.PFR/Boost.Describe adapters) enables automatic mapping without a manual json_data_contract
integration.platforms: any C++17 target; optional SIMD member-skip paths for x86 SSE4.2/AVX2 and arm NEON, but README says the default constexpr (non-SIMD) path is generally faster
integration.thread_safety: Parsing has no shared mutable state across calls; the custom error-handler function pointer (`daw_json_error_handler`) is thread_local, so it must be installed per thread rather than once globally
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — from_json/to_json call shape resembles RapidJSON's, but every mapped type needs a json_data_contract specialization (or a reflection-based adapter); it is not a header swap

gotchas: Struct member order should match JSON key order; mismatches force backtracking and slow parsing
Missing/optional members slow parsing more than explicit nulls do, per the README's performance notes
Exceptions are on by default (throws daw::json::json_exception); disabling them (or building with -fno-exceptions) falls back to std::terminate unless a custom thread_local handler is installed
Duplicate JSON member names resolve to an unspecified one unless you explicitly use json_key_value to preserve or order all of them
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over cjson.cpp/json.cpp/Tachyon.JSON/utl::json when you want direct-to-typed-struct parsing (no DOM, constructor-arg based) plus SAX/lazy-pull/NDJSON modes from one mapping, not just a faster nlohmann-shaped DOM. If raw throughput against simdjson On-Demand is the only metric, that (or Tachyon.JSON, which also beats simdjson On-Demand in its own table) is faster than DAW JSON Link here.
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks Json test (parse + sum values from a generated coordinates JSON file) run on gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 (libc++), -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c++23, Intel Xeon E-2324G: DAW JSON Link 0.089s (g++) / 0.085s (clang++) beats RapidJSON 0.154s/0.194s (1.73x/2.28x), simdjson DOM 0.107s (1.20x), Boost.JSON 0.374s (4.2x) and nlohmann 1.266s (14.2x); simdjson On-Demand (0.060s) is faster than DAW. Memory column shows +0.00 MiB over baseline for DAW versus +175 MiB (simdjson DOM) and +96 MiB (gason), evidencing the no-parser-allocation claim. Older author-run tables (2015-2017 CPUs, gcc 9.2.1) showed 0.19s vs RapidJSON's 0.53s and 0.11s vs 0.26s, both independently confirmed.
